title: Global Solution of Integer, Stochastic and Nonconvex Optimization Problems: SS Dey et al.
contribution: Editorial preface (Dey, Luedtke, Sahinidis) dedicating a 29-paper Math. Program. B issue to Shabbir Ahmed and grouping the papers by his three research areas.
problem_entry: Integer, stochastic and nonconvex problems are expressive but mostly NP-hard; the issue celebrates methods giving exact or provably approximate solutions at practical scale (p. 1).
key_idea: Use Ahmed's body of work (MILP/MINLP; stochastic/robust/DRO; multi-stage) as the organising frame for the issue (pp. 2-5).
positioning: Credits Ahmed's pairing inequalities as predating multi-row cuts and lists his MINLP lines, several coauthored with Dey (pp. 2, 5-7).
writing: Joint three-editor voice; explicit conflict-of-interest paragraph on how editor-coauthored papers were handled (p. 5).

method_links.note: weak: editorial values exact or provably approximate solutions; shared editorial voice

transferable: When guest-editing, state in the preface how papers coauthored by an editor were handled and by whom (p. 5).
coauthors: J. R. Luedtke, N. V. Sahinidis

quotes.text: A common theme in Ahmed’s work is his invention of methods that enable practical computational solution of theoretically intractable problems.
Despite this challenge, there has been tremendous advances in computational methods that can provide exact or provably approximate solutions to these problems at scales of practical interest.

title: Lower bounds on the size of general branch-and-bound trees
contribution: Exponential lower bounds, independent of branching-coefficient size, on general (split-disjunction) branch-and-bound trees for packing, set-cover, perturbed cross-polytope (ruling out polynomial smoothed analysis) and TSP instances.
problem_entry: Open question of Beame et al. on superpolynomial lower bounds for general branching, partly settled by Dadush-Tiwari for the cross-polytope; motivated by solver difficulty of instances needing exponential trees (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Define BB hardness/BBdepth/BBrank as analogues of CG rank and transfer lower bounds between problems through integral affine maps (flipping, embedding, duplication) (pp. 6-11).
assumptions: B&B abstracted as a full binary tree of legal integer disjunctions without the usual LP-optimum and pruning requirements, which strengthens lower bounds (p. 6); packing/cover instances have exponentially many constraints (p. 4).
proof_devices: BB rank lower-bounds BB hardness via hyperplane separation (Lemma 1, p. 7)
simulation lemma for integral affine maps and hardness lemma (Lemmas 5-6, pp. 8-10)
generalised Dadush-Tiwari lemma via Helly's theorem: |D|/n leaves (Lemma 7, p. 11)
midpoint argument: 2^n leaves for the cross-polytope (Proposition 3, p. 14)
Gaussian tail + union bound + Sauer-Shelah + binary entropy for the perturbed cross-polytope (Theorem 2, pp. 16-17)
composition with Cook-Dash construction for TSP (Proposition 6, Corollary 8, p. 18)
positioning: Presents itself as the branch-and-bound analog of Chvatal-Cook-Hartmann CG-rank lower bounds (p. 1); improves Dadush-Tiwari's 2^n/n to 2^n and removes the coefficient dependence of Fleming et al. (pp. 4-5).
writing: Contributions paragraph followed by a numbered comparison with the two closest results (pp. 4-5); no conclusion section.
limits_future: Instances use exponentially many constraints, so the Dadush-Tiwari question for polynomially described polytopes stays open (p. 4); extends to branch-and-cut with split-like cuts via Basu et al. (p. 5).

method_links.note: studies solver tree size because exponential-tree instances are likely hard for MILP solvers
boundary stated next to the result: exponential constraint count, coefficient independence, smoothed analysis ruled out
import is from cutting-plane rank theory into branch-and-bound rather than MILP into QCQP

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: transfer hardness through integral affine maps
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: BBdepth is preserved by integral affine one-to-one maps; one hard base polytope (cross-polytope) yields set-cover and TSP bounds

transferable: Define a depth/rank notion for separating one point, prove integral affine one-to-one maps cannot decrease it, then reduce each new problem to one hard base polytope (pp. 8-10).
Apply Helly's theorem per leaf: each leaf uses at most n original constraints, so if every constraint in D is needed for infeasibility at least |D|/n leaves are required (p. 11).
To rule out a smoothed-analysis upper bound, perturb coefficients with Gaussian noise and show by union bounds that infeasibility and many half-integral points both survive (pp. 16-17).

quotes.text: In contrast, in this paper we provide lower bounds for the size of general branch-and-bound tree for packing and set-cover instances, which are more natural combinatorial problems than those mentioned above.
We note that the packing and covering instances are described using an exponential number of constraints

title: Solving sparse principal component analysis with global support
contribution: Operator-norm convex relaxations of the row-sparse orthonormal set with O(sqrt(log r)) and 2sqrt(r) hull-approximation factors, and a convex integer program giving dual bounds for sparse PCA with global support with multiplicative/additive guarantees, tested up to 2000x2000.
problem_entry: Existing SPCAgs methods are heuristics with guarantees only under statistical models or stationary-point methods; none certifies quality against dual bounds (abstract p. 1; pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Relax F by norm constraints with provable factors (CR1, CR1', CR2) and handle the non-concave objective with SOS-II piecewise-linear overestimators, giving a convex IP whose bound is within rho^2 opt plus an additive term <= Tr(A) r/(4N^2) (pp. 4-6, 18-19).
assumptions: Model-free (no statistical model, p. 4); A PSD; Lemma 1 assumes k >= 40, small k covered by Theorem 3 (p. 9); l2->1 norm NP-hard, motivating CR1' (p. 5).
proof_devices: random row sparsification with Pietsch-Grothendieck factorization weights, unbiased with controlled operator norm (pp. 10-11)
SOS-II piecewise-linear upper approximation of squared linear forms on [-theta_j, theta_j] (pp. 18-19)
experiments: Spiked-covariance artificial (d=500) and real CovColon/Lymph/Reddit instances up to 2000x2000; gap to best of 400 greedy restarts; CIP best on 26 of 42 small instances, SDP then dropped; sub-matrix technique for large instances, only slightly better than trivial Baseline 1 on CovColon/Lymph but much better on Reddit (pp. 23-30).
positioning: Five-category survey of sparse PCA work; generalises the r=1 dual-bound result of [19] (pp. 3-4, 6).
writing: Main theorems stated in the introduction before proofs (pp. 4-6); journal version notes new results and completely revamped experiments over the preliminary version (p. 7); reviewers credited for the SDP and a heuristic (p. 31).
limits_future: Some instances still need more techniques to close the gap; no comparable model-free results exist (p. 30).

method_links.note: dual bound from SOC/convex-IP relaxation, gap reported at 2000x2000 scale on a laptop
explicit approximation factor for each relaxation; hardness of l2->1 norm and of CRi-Relax stated
no exact optimum available; yardstick is own primal heuristic; 100x100 submatrices used as first rung

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: convex-IP dual bound for convex maximisation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: norm-ball relaxation of the sparse set plus SOS-II piecewise-linear overestimate of each quadratic term gives a convex IP with additive error O(1/N^2); reused in S064

transferable: For convex maximisation over a sparse set, relax the set with provable-factor norm constraints and overestimate each squared linear form by an SOS-II piecewise-linear function; the convex IP bound has additive error shrinking as 1/N^2 (pp. 6, 18-19).
Prove a hull-approximation factor by comparing support functions and exhibiting a randomly sparsified point with sampling weights from a factorization matched to the controlled norm (pp. 9-11).
Report the small-instance comparison with an expensive dominated baseline in full, then say why it is dropped for larger instances (p. 27).

quotes.text: Recall that dual bounds are typically crucial for effective computational procedures for non-convex problems, which are usually solved using branch-and-bound type algorithms that use dual bounds to prune the solution space.
These problems are quite challenging, and in some instances, we still need more techniques to close the gap.

title: Variable selection for kernel two-sample tests
contribution: Variance-regularised MMD variable selection for two-sample testing, with an exact MISDP/outer-approximation algorithm and approximation algorithms with ratios for the sparse trust-region subproblem, plus kernel-specific sample-size and power rates.
problem_entry: Selecting the d most informative of D variables to distinguish two distributions; prior approaches are parametric or Bonferroni-based, and sparse logistic regression can fail (pp. 2-3, 7).
key_idea: Maximise MMD^2 - lambda sigma^2 as a surrogate for the power-optimal ratio; linear kernel reduces to the sparse trust-region subproblem (STRS), solved exactly by a strengthened MISDP with outer approximation or approximately by SDP/ADMM, truncation, or an l1-relaxation convex IP (pp. 5, 7, 10-14).
assumptions: A PSD w.l.o.g. by eigenvalue shift (p. 7); lambda by cross-validation (p. 5); kernel-specific data structure Assumption 1 (p. 15); bounded Lipschitz kernels (EC.1, p. 38, statement only).
proof_devices: rank-1 SDP exactness for the MISDP reformulation (Theorem 1, p. 10)
saddle-point reformulation with sup-gradients enabling outer approximation (Theorem 2, Algorithm 3, pp. 11-12)
extension of a=0 sparse-PCA approximation-ratio proofs to inhomogeneous objectives (Theorems 3-5, pp. 12-14)
sample-size rates Omega(d^2 log(D/d)), Omega(d^4 log(D/d)), Omega(d log(D/d)) and O(n_Te^{-1/2}) type-II error (Proposition 3, Theorems 6-7, pp. 15-16)
experiments: STRS algorithms vs ground truth on four synthetic families (100 trials) with timing; testing power vs n and D; FDP/NDP support recovery; MNIST and sepsis (quadratic MMD power 0.915); projected Wasserstein wins the Gaussian-mixture case (pp. 17-24).
positioning: Positions against parametric variable selection and classifier-based tests; builds on kernel-selection MMD work [44,59] and sparse-PCA formulations [40,8,21] (pp. 2-3, 11, 14).
writing: Contribution bullets split into computational and statistical views plus their trade-off (p. 2); unresolved placeholder 'xxx' left in Proposition 3 of v4 (p. 15).
limits_future: Theory for kernel hyperparameters and support recovery, faster algorithms (p. 24); Gaussian kernel statistically best but hardest to optimise (p. 2).

method_links.note: approximation algorithms ranked against ground truth before downstream use
approximation ratios for each algorithm and hardness of constant ratio cited
relaxation machinery reused but deliverable is testing power, not a certified gap; Dey's share of the work not stated

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: convex-IP dual bound for convex maximisation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: l1-norm relaxation plus convex integer program adopted from [21, Section 2.2] for STRS

transferable: Before using an approximation algorithm downstream, compare it with the exact optimum on small synthetic instances over many trials and tabulate time beside quality (pp. 17-18).
Replace a hard fractional signal/standard-deviation objective by signal minus lambda times variance, tuning lambda by cross-validation (p. 5).
Show a baseline's failure with a population example in which its statistic is identically zero (Example 1, p. 7).

quotes.text: While the Gaussian kernel requires a smaller sample size to be statistically powerful, the corresponding MMD optimization is challenging.
Since the convex integer programming algorithm has satisfactory performance with relatively fast computational speed, we recommend using this approximation algorithm when solving (STRS).

title: Lifting convex inequalities for bipartite bilinear programs
contribution: Lifting theory for convex seed inequalities over one bipartite bilinear constraint: lifting is always possible at bounds, a subadditive framework for sequence-independent lifting, an SOC-representable bilinear cover inequality within factor 4 of the hull, and a closed-form lifted bilinear cover inequality.
problem_entry: Lifting drove MILP cuts but is rare for nonlinear sets; by analogy with knapsack single-row cuts, study one nonconvex quadratic row with bounds (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Port sequential and subadditive sequence-independent lifting (Gu-Nemhauser-Savelsbergh) to separable bipartite bilinear sets, using a minimal-cover seed (bilinear cover inequality) with a two-slope subadditive bound on its lifting function (pp. 4-8).
assumptions: Variables in [0,1] fixed at bounds (Example 3 shows failure at interior values, p. 4); separability for sequence independence (p. 4); minimal-cover partition exists, otherwise conv(Q) is polyhedral (Theorem 2, p. 6).
proof_devices: extreme-point characterisation reduces lifting to three-variable case analysis (Theorem 1, p. 4)
subadditive upper bound on the lifting function implies sequence-independent validity (Proposition 1, p. 5)
disjunctive programming, extended formulation and approximate Fourier-Motzkin projection (Theorem 3, p. 6)
factor-4 hull sandwich via linear optimisation with nonnegative objectives (Theorem 4, p. 7)
exact lifting function near the origin extended by a global linear bound (Theorem 5, p. 7)
positioning: Lists the few nonlinear lifting papers and claims to be first for general nonconvex quadratic constraints with arbitrary variable count; strengthens the known inequality for the set without upper bounds ([53]) (pp. 2, 6).
writing: Main results section with all theorem statements before proofs; motivating examples precede theorems; explicit future-directions section (pp. 3-9).
limits_future: Characterise lifting with non-affine forms, non-separable sequence independence, separation complexity and computational value (pp. 8-9); Theorem 1's algorithm not necessarily practical (p. 4).

method_links.note: MILP lifting, subadditivity, minimal covers and knapsack-first analogy carried to a single bilinear row
counterexamples for dropped hypotheses, dichotomy theorem, factor-4 hull approximation

transferable: Write each lifting coefficient as a sup problem and check finiteness by splitting the fixed variable's range and using extreme-point structure (Example 1, p. 3).
Justify a seed inequality by a hull-approximation factor, not only dominance (Theorem 4, p. 7).
Pair each positive lifting theorem with small counterexamples for each hypothesis (Examples 2-4, pp. 3-4, 8-9).

quotes.text: Generating valid inequalities for single row relaxations (together with bounds and integrality restrictions), i.e., for knapsack constraints, was the first, and arguably the most important step in the development of computationally useful cutting-planes in MILP.
Finally, extensive numerical experiments should be conducted to understand the practical strength of these inequalities and to determine how useful they can be in the solution of QCQPs.

title: A covering decomposition algorithm for power grid cyber-network segmentation
contribution: SIAM OP23 talk (slides) on a covering-decomposition algorithm for a trilevel designer-attacker-defender model of SCADA network segmentation that drops the invulnerability and design-independent attacker-region assumptions.
problem_entry: Trilevel interdiction: segment the grid's communication network to minimise worst-case load shed; prior methods assume invulnerable assets or design-independent attacker feasibility (pp. 2, 19).
key_idea: Adapt Israeli-Wood covering decomposition, alternating designs with lower bounds and worst-case attacks with upper bounds; relax inner DC-OPF to capacitated network flow (pp. 24-27).
assumptions: Example budgets: attack 7, BA/CC 3, substation 1; load shed 119.2 MW to 75.4 MW (pp. 5, 13-14).
experiments: 2000-bus and 500-bus cases (pp. 31-32; plots not extracted, not read).
positioning: Classifies bilevel/trilevel interdiction algorithms and cites Johnson and Dey (IJOC 2022) for the network-flow restriction (pp. 16-18, 24).
writing: Slide deck; conclusions and future directions as separate slides (pp. 33-34).
limits_future: Constraint programming for the feasibility problem, Benders for large attacker problems, Version 1 for early termination with a gap (p. 34).

method_links.note: bounding via a tractable restriction and alternating bounds, not a cheap convex relaxation; Dey's share not separable

transferable: When an inner model lacks valid dual-variable bounds, replace it by a tractable restriction (network flow without Ohm's law) and state which bound property survives (p. 24).
coauthors: E. S. Johnson, J. Eckstein, C. A. Phillips, J. D. Siirola

quotes.text: We’ve lost nothing: All we had was a lower bound anyway because we don’t know valid bounds on the dual variables of DCOPF!
Increases in the substation budget do not help the network designer significantly, and come at high computational cost

title: Integer programming and combinatorial optimization (IPCO) 2021
contribution: Two-page editorial preface (Dey, Singh, Williamson) to the Math. Program. B special issue of 26 journal versions of IPCO 2021 papers.
problem_entry: Collect full journal versions of the 33 accepted IPCO 2021 extended abstracts (from 90+ submissions) (p. 1).
key_idea: Journal versions add full proofs, extensions and details over the extended abstracts (p. 2).

quotes.text: These papers that now appear represent a snapshot of the very best of an exciting and vibrant domain within mathematical optimization.

title: Modeling and Solving the Large Scale EV Charger Location Planning Problem
contribution: City-scale MIP models for EV fast-charger location with home-or-work service radius, budget and two equity constraints, solved for Atlanta with census commuter data.
problem_entry: Prior siting uses heuristics on small candidate sets and the US standard EVI-Pro is a simulation; equity absent from location models (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Facility-location MIP where each origin-destination commuter type may be served near home or work, with five variants (serve-all, budgeted, two 40% equity rules) and a continuous-assignment relaxation rounded down (pp. 3-7).
assumptions: Charging only near origin/destination within 1 mile; 250 miles per charger-hour, 12 h/day; 2-SD outlier removal; home-charging by housing type; CEJST status remapped to 2020 tracts (pp. 4, 9-11); formulation inconsistencies in capacity coefficient (2m vs m), constraint (7) description and z domain (pp. 4-5, 7).
experiments: Atlanta: 1,518 tracts, 326,579 commuter types; Gurobi to 1% gap on the relaxation with rounding; Serve-All 41,423 chargers; equity constraints cost little below 4,000 chargers and make placements grow monotonically (pp. 7, 11-17).
positioning: Contrasts with GA-based siting and the EVI-Pro simulation; recommends using both (pp. 2, 18).
writing: Four numbered contribution claims (p. 3); reports a counterintuitive result (constrained model slightly better) and attributes it to the 1% gap (p. 15).
limits_future: Time-of-day demand, grid load, Level 2, non-car modes (p. 18); 'optimal solutions' claim rests on a rounded relaxation solved to 1% gap (pp. 3, 7, 11-12).

method_links.note: reported gap is the 1% gap of a rounded relaxation, not a certificate for the stated model

transferable: When comparing solutions across budgets, check whether independent solves move facilities back and forth, and report a constraint that makes placements grow monotonically as a planning property (pp. 15-17).
Bracket an unknown behavioural parameter by solving both extremes (nobody versus everybody able charges at home) to get upper and lower bounds on facilities needed (pp. 10-11).

quotes.text: To the best of our knowledge, none of the above models are able to provide optimal solutions at the scale of a full city, without resorting to greedy algorithms or other heuristic methods.
This is an understandable but undesirable result of independent solves of the model.
